text.tspan: Democracy: Progress and Pillars
The Big Picture: Democracy Over Time
What drives democracy?
Economic of Growth
I pool all country from 1970–2024 and compare
the distribution of annual real GDP growth by
regime type. Median growth rates are broadly
similar across regimes, while closed autocracies
show a slightly higher median. The main
difference is volatility: autocracies exhibit much
wider dispersion, with both rapid booms and
deep contractions, while democracies show
tighter distributions and fewer severe downturns.
After showing how different types of regimes
perform differently, I plot each country’s average
annual real GDP growth (2014–2024) against its
change in level of democracy over the same period
to test whether growth leads to democracy. The
bold axis mark 0% growth and zero democratic
change. These points are clustered near the origin,
especially for democracies. Therefore, there is no
link between short-run growth and democratic
gains but other factors likely matter more.
Since 1970, the global level of liberal democracy climbed, surged after the Cold War, peaked around
2010, and has since flattened with a slight dip. This project traces that arc and asks a simple question:
what moves democracy? The following visualizations take a closer look.
Freedom of Expression
Definition: The extent to which people and
media can speak, publish, and access
information without censorship or
intimidation.
What we see: Strong, non-linear positive
association with democracy (r≈0.86). The
points are clustered by different regime type.
More free countries are more closely
clustered while non-free ones are separately
widely. Its noticeable threshold around 0.65
level of freedom on expression, once
countries pass it, democracy level rises
steeply.
Resource Equality
Definition: The degree to which public resources,
services, and opportunities are allocated fairly
across groups and regions without favoritism or
elite capture. I use Equal Distribution Index (0–1;
higher = more equal), averaged over 2014–2024,
and plotted against the level of democracy.
What we see: The LOESS trend rises throughout:
moving from low to mid equality is associated with
steady gains in democratic quality, and beyond
0.85 the slope steepens and high-democracy cases
cluster. Overall the relationship is clearly positive.
Having shown the overall
association, I then check whether it
holds year by year. The three small
multiples (2014, 2019, 2024) plot
country averages with a LOESS
trend. The curve’s shape is
strikingly consistent across time:
gradual gains from low→mid
equality and a steeper rise beyond
0.8. Only 2024 sits slightly lower at
mid-equality, consistent with mild
democratic backsliding.
Takeaway
This four-panel view places the factors side-by-side using country averages (2014–2024) with LOESS
trends. GDP growth shows little relationship with democracy: flat and noisy. Resource equality rises
steadily with democracy and steepens at high equality, suggesting a threshold effect. Freedom of
expression exhibits a strong, nonlinear association—big democracy gains appear once expressive
rights move beyond low levels, then taper at the top. Rule of law tracks democracy almost linearly
across the range, the tightest, most consistent pattern of the four.
Taken together with the long-run picture: an upswing through the 1990s, then a plateau and mild
backsliding since the mid-2010s; the evidence suggests that democracy rises and falls less with GDP
booms than with institutional openings and protections. Looking ahead, trajectories hinge on
shoring up core guardrails: independent courts and anticorruption, expressive freedoms and media
pluralism, and fair access to state resources. Headwinds include polarization and disinformation, AI-
enabled surveillance, executive overreach, external shocks, and inequality. The task is to keep rights
intact in downturns and translate growth into accountable institutions.
Data Source: V-Dem Dataset and World Bank WDI: real GDP growth
The Liberal Democracy Index (V-
Dem) aggregates expert-coded
indicators on elections, rights,
media, rule of law, and checks on
the executive. It ranges from 0–1
(higher = more liberal democracy).
The chart shows the unweighted
global average by year.
Slow rise through the 1970s–80s.
Step jump 1989–93 with post–Cold
War transitions.
Gradual gains in the 2000s.
Peak ~2010–12, then a flat/slight
decline (mid-2010s backsliding).
What changed (1970–2024)
After overview, I aksed where the change in
democracy comes from. To probe this, I
grouped countries into four broad buckets and
plotted their regional averages over time.
West Europe + USA: high & stable; mild
Latin America: big surge mid-1980s–90s;
Ex-Soviet: very low until 1990–92 jump, then
Rest of World: steady gains to 2010; then
Democracy in 2024: Balance of Regimes
Competitive, free, and fair multiparty elections plus strong
liberal guarantees: rule of law, judicial independence,
constraints on the executive, media freedom, and protection
of civil & minority rights.
Elections meet basic standards of competitiveness,
inclusiveness, and integrity, but liberal checks are weaker or
uneven (courts, media, civil liberties, minority protections).
Multiparty elections exist in form but not in substance with
systematic bias, repression, fraud, or media capture prevent
genuine contestation.
No meaningful multiparty competition for chief executive
and legislature. Civil liberties and organization are tightly
restricted.
Rule of law
Definition: The extent to which clear, public
laws are applied equally and predictably by
independent courts without arbitrary power or
corruption. Such concept is best thought of as an
institutional stage, so I bucket countries into
quintiles on the Rule of Law index (lowest →
highest) rather than treating it as a single point
estimate.
What we see: Each bar reports the mean level
of Democracy within that quintile. Stronger rule
of law coincides with substantially higher
democratic quality.
